findings.title: FEIE claimed but the taxpayer does not qualify
findings.detail: Form 2555 exclusion was claimed in Layer 1, but the §911 tests fail: tax home is in the US; neither the bona-fide-residence nor the physical-presence test is met. FEIE is only available to someone living abroad — a US-based taxpayer with foreign income must use the Foreign Tax Credit instead. The engine has computed US tax WITHOUT the exclusion.
findings.recommendation: Remove the FEIE claim and rely on Form 1116 FTC for the Indian taxes (usually better anyway when Indian rates exceed US rates). If the taxpayer genuinely lives abroad, complete the tax-home and presence-test fields in the US Layer 1 so the exclusion can be applied.

findings.title: Foreign Tax Credit shortfall — residual double taxation
findings.detail: Indian tax paid ($22,837) exceeds the US FTC limitation ($13,544) for this year. $9,293 of Indian tax cannot be credited currently and would otherwise be double-taxed.
findings.recommendation: $9,293 is eligible to carry over under §904(c) (back 1 year / forward 10), but WISING is a single-year snapshot — it does NOT persist this carryover across tax years or track it for you. Record $9,293 on Form 1116 Schedule B this year, and re-enter it as prior-year carryover when you run next year's numbers. Also check whether treaty re-sourcing (Art. 25) could reclassify some income to lift the limitation — WISING does not test this automatically.

findings.title: Missing documentation is costing $512 in avoidable withholding tax this year
findings.detail: Adding up every income stream where a treaty-reduced rate was claimed but denied for lack of supporting documentation: ₹42,500 in India (TRC/Form 41) — $512 total, computed directly from the same rate/amount figures used elsewhere on this page, not estimated. See the Withholding Taxes page for the full row-by-row breakdown of which income and which document.
findings.recommendation: File the missing documentation (TRC + Form 41 for India s.159 elections; Form W-8BEN with the US withholding agent for FDAP) as soon as possible — none of this is lost once filed for a FUTURE payment, but the tax already withheld/assessed on past payments this year may require a separate refund claim to recover.

findings.title: Treaty relief claimed without supporting documents
findings.detail: A treaty position / DTAA rate is being relied upon, but Form 41 is not on file. Indian tax authorities will deny treaty relief u/s 159(8) without a valid TRC, and Form 41 is mandatory u/r 75.
findings.recommendation: Obtain Form 41 before filing. For US residents, request Form 6166 from the IRS (Form 8802 application) well in advance — it can take 6–8 weeks.

findings.title: Unexplained income on file (s.195) — not reflected in the India tax computed above
findings.detail: ₹2,50,000 is recorded as unexplained income under s.195. This carries a flat ~39% effective rate (30% tax + 25% surcharge + 4% cess, per Finance Act 2026) and — unlike any other provision — denies every deduction, exemption, and loss set-off with no exceptions. The India tax figure above does not include this; it needs to be added separately.
findings.recommendation: Compute the s.195 addition separately at the full ~39% effective rate before relying on the India tax total above, and confirm the source of these funds is genuinely unexplained rather than misclassified income that belongs under a normal head.

findings.title: PFIC exposure: Indian mutual funds
findings.detail: 2 Indian mutual fund / ETF holding(s) detected. For a US person these are Passive Foreign Investment Companies — taxed under the punitive §1291 excess-distribution regime by default, with a separate Form 8621 per fund.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate a QEF or Mark-to-Market election (must be timely). Many Indian AMCs cannot supply a PFIC Annual Information Statement, which can force the §1291 default — consider restructuring holdings to US-domiciled funds.

findings.title: FBAR threshold breached
findings.detail: Aggregate peak balance across foreign accounts is $54,217, above the USD 10,000 reporting cliff. EVERY foreign account must be reported, not just those over the limit.
findings.recommendation: File FinCEN Form 114 by the due date (auto-extended to Oct 15). Non-willful penalties start at ~$10,000 per violation; willful penalties are far higher.

findings.title: New York state income tax: $14,797 (Form IT-201)
findings.detail: New York taxes a full-year resident's WORLDWIDE income, including Indian-source income already reported on the federal and Indian returns — computed here as $265,626 of state taxable income (federal AGI $281,676 less the New York standard deduction) at New York's own bracket rates. Neither the Foreign Tax Credit computed above nor any DTAA relief applies here — New York is not a party to the India-US treaty and does not treat Indian tax as a creditable state-level offset.
findings.recommendation: File Form IT-201 alongside the federal return. This is a full-year-resident, TY2025-rates estimate — it does not split state-source income for a part-year or nonresident allocation, does not model New York's own AGI addition/subtraction adjustments beyond the standard deduction, and (for California) does not include the local-jurisdiction SDI/VPDI payroll tax. Treat as directional, not filing-ready.

findings.title: $2,169 of lottery/gaming winnings — flat 30% (s.128/194), no exemptions
findings.detail: This income is taxed at a flat 30% with no basic exemption threshold, no Chapter VI-A deduction and no §156 rebate — it's now included in the India tax total and the FTC/double-tax figures above. Because the US taxes worldwide income, the same winnings are very likely also US-taxable as ordinary income — a real double-tax exposure that the general FTC computation only approximates, since it doesn't specifically match this flat 30% Indian rate against whatever ordinary rate the US applies to it.
findings.recommendation: Confirm US-side treatment of the same winnings separately from the general FTC computation — a flat-rate/graduated-rate mismatch on the same income can leave a residual gap the average-rate FTC approximation misses.

findings.title: NIIT / Additional Medicare surtaxes are not offset by the Foreign Tax Credit
findings.detail: NIIT $1,204 (§1411, 3.8%) applies on top of regular US income tax. Indian income tax can only credit the REGULAR US income tax (§901/§904) — these two surtaxes are outside the FTC mechanism entirely, so they stand as double taxation even when the rest of the Indian tax is fully credited.
findings.recommendation: There is no credit path for this residue — the only levers are reducing MAGI/net investment income (retirement contributions, timing) or, for Additional Medicare, W-4 withholding planning. Make sure the client understands the FTC reconciliation above does not clear this amount.

findings.title: Advance-tax interest exposure — ss.424/425 (₹95,258)
findings.detail: Advance tax paid (₹0) falls short of the assessed tax (₹14,65,501) this year. At 1%/month simple interest: ₹58,620 under s.424 (shortfall below the 90% floor, 4 months to the non-audit (31 Jul) due date) + ₹36,638 under s.425 (quarter-by-quarter installment shortfalls). Both keep accruing past the due date until actually paid — this is the exposure AS OF the due date, not a final number.
findings.recommendation: Pay the shortfall before filing to stop s.424 interest accruing further; s.425's quarter-by-quarter amount is fixed once the year ends and doesn't grow. If the year isn't over yet, revise the remaining installment(s) upward.

findings.title: 2 DTAA treaty rate election(s) on file
findings.detail: Layer 1 records a claimed treaty rate on the following India-source income stream(s): interest @ 15% (Art 11(2)(b)) on ₹1,50,000 [election denied — TRC/Form 41 missing, ordinary slab rates apply to this slice instead]; royalty @ 15% (Art 12(2)(a)(ii)) on ₹4,00,000 [election denied — domestic 20% rate applied instead, TRC/Form 41 missing]. Dividend, royalty and FTS elections are compared against the flat domestic s.207 rate (s.159, whichever is lower). Interest is different — ordinary NRO interest isn't actually s.207 income (that concessional rate is narrow, foreign-currency-borrowing interest only), so it's slab-rate income by default, and an election only helps when the flat treaty rate beats the marginal slab rate on that specific slice. Capital-gains elections are NOT applied — Art. 13 itself provides no special treaty rate, domestic law governs regardless (see Part H). Layer 1 does NOT show Form 41 on file — every one of these elections is at risk of being denied and defaulting back to slab/domestic rates without it.
findings.recommendation: Obtain Form 41 before relying on any of these elected rates — without it, the payer/assessing officer can withhold or assess at the full domestic rate shown above instead.

findings.title: No US–India Totalization Agreement — self-employment tax has no double-coverage relief
findings.detail: $5,750 of US self-employment tax (Schedule SE) is owed in full. Unlike ~30 countries with a US Totalization Agreement, India has none — there is no Certificate of Coverage to exempt a self-employed or seconded worker from social-security-style contributions in both countries, and no credit mechanism folds Indian PF/social contributions into the US SE tax computation.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether Indian-side EPF/social contributions are also being made on the same work; if so this is uncoordinated double coverage by design (not a filing error) — the only mitigants are entity structuring (e.g., routing through a foreign corporation to convert SE income to a dividend/salary mix) or accepting the cost.

findings.title: State tax residency is not resolved by the DTAA / federal treaty position (NY)
findings.detail: The India-US treaty and the federal residency determination above bind FEDERAL tax only. NY applies its own domicile or statutory-day residency test, independent of the Article 4 tie-breaker or any §911/1040NR position. A taxpayer can be a federal treaty non-resident while remaining a full worldwide-income STATE resident with Indian income fully taxable and no matching relief in some states.
findings.recommendation: Run the state's own residency test (domicile intent + day count) separately from the federal/treaty analysis. New York statutory-residency facts are on file (183-day + permanent-abode / 548-day rule) — NY residency is tested independently of the federal position. Do not assume the federal treaty position carries over.

findings.title: 5 income head(s) taxed under both codes — see reconciliation
findings.detail: The same income is taxed in India (its own Act) and the US (the IRC): Business / Professional, House property / Rental, Interest, Dividend, Capital gains. Overlapping exposure of $75,082 is what the FTC / §159 relief resolves. Some heads are planning-grade estimates pending line-item inputs.
findings.recommendation: Open the Cross-Basis Reconciliation on the Filings tab to see each head on both bases, then relieve the overlap via Form 1116 (US) / Form 44 (India).

findings.title: Form 44 — required for the Indian FTC claim
findings.detail: Foreign income / foreign tax is present, so India requires Form 44 (with Schedule FSI and TR) on or before the ITR due date to allow FTC u/s 90/91.
findings.recommendation: WISING flags Form 44 (with Schedule FSI/TR) as required on the filing checklist, using the FSI/TR figures already computed above — actually preparing and e-filing it on the income-tax portal ahead of the ITR due date is still a manual step.

findings.title: Tax-year apportionment: Indian FY ↔ US CY (computed)
findings.detail: India taxes Apr–Mar; the US taxes Jan–Dec. WISING splits the Indian FY across US calendar years — $61,353 into CY2026 and $20,451 into CY2027 (Indian quarterly data) — and apportions the US calendar year into the Indian FY (9/12 + 3/12).
findings.recommendation: See the FY ↔ CY Apportionment panel on the Filings tab for the period-matched figures behind Form 44 (India) and Form 1116 (US). Planning-grade — refine with per-transaction dates at filing.

findings.title: FX conversion basis is an approximation
findings.detail: Cross-border amounts are normalized at a flat 83 INR/USD. Statutory FTC computations require the telegraphic-transfer buying rate on the relevant date (Rule 115 / SBI TTBR).
findings.recommendation: Re-price each foreign income and tax item at the correct per-transaction rate before filing; the flat rate is for planning visibility only.

findings.title: Indian company held below the 10% CFC threshold
findings.detail: 3 Indian business interest(s) on file, but Layer 1 shows US ownership below 10% — so Form 5471 Category 5 / GILTI do not apply this year.
findings.recommendation: No 5471 action needed at current ownership. WISING recomputes this every time you re-run the numbers, so update the ownership percentage in Layer 1 as soon as a purchase or reorganization changes it — this isn't monitored in the background.

documents.desc: Application to the IRS for Form 6166 — the US residency certificate India's TRC requirement expects the other contracting state to issue.
documents.why: DTAA relief is being claimed on Indian-source income — Form 6166 must be requested via Form 8802 before it can be filed with the Indian TRC/Form 41 paperwork; IRS processing typically takes 4-6+ weeks, so file well ahead of the India due date.

documents.why: Indian income is on file for this taxpayer — TDS, advance tax and reported high-value transactions should be cross-checked against these statements before the return is filed.

documents.name: Form 16 / Form 16A (TDS Certificates)

documents.why: Indian income subject to TDS is on file — hold the certificate from each deductor to reconcile against Form 26AS/AIS and support the credit claimed in the ITR.

documents.name: LRS Form A2 (Outward Remittance Declaration)

documents.why: Outward remittances under LRS were made this year — each remittance requires its own Form A2 filed with the bank at the time of transfer, separate from the annual Form 145/146 (was 15CA/15CB) return-time reporting.

scopeNotes.title: GAAR is not evaluated
scopeNotes.body: India's General Anti-Avoidance Rule can recharacterize arrangements that lack commercial substance — a facts-and-circumstances judgment no rules engine can safely make. WISING flags mechanical conflicts only; whether an arrangement invites GAAR scrutiny remains a professional call.

scopeNotes.title: STT is not computed as a levy
scopeNotes.body: Securities Transaction Tax charged on trades (raised on F&O by Finance Act 2026) isn't calculated here. The stt_paid flag on each transaction drives the capital-gains regime (s.196/198 vs s.197) — the levy amount itself is neither a tax credit nor a capital-gains deduction, so nothing downstream depends on it.

scopeNotes.title: Your obligations as a TDS deductor aren't tracked
scopeNotes.body: The Withholding page covers tax withheld FROM this taxpayer's income. Duties in the opposite direction — deducting TDS on payments the business makes to vendors, contractors, or professionals — aren't monitored as a compliance obligation in their own right, though the resulting s.40(a) expense disallowance for TDS failures (and s.40A(3) cash-payment / s.43B(h) MSME-overdue disallowances) does flow into business income (Phase 1).

scopeNotes.title: Clubbing amounts are taken as entered
scopeNotes.body: Spousal and minor-child clubbed income entered in Layer 1 is taxed as given. WISING doesn't trace asset transfers between family members to detect clubbing that should have been reported but wasn't.

scopeNotes.title: FICA/FUTA levies aren't computed
scopeNotes.body: Employee and employer Social Security/Medicare/unemployment payroll taxes are a separate tax base from income tax. Only the pieces that touch the 1040 are computed: Additional Medicare 0.9%, self-employment tax, and the W-2 withholding shown on the Withholding page.

scopeNotes.title: FATCA Chapter 4 withholding is institution-side
scopeNotes.body: The 30% FATCA withholding regime (IRC §§1471-1474) applies to payments to non-compliant foreign financial institutions — banks' problem, not yours directly. Where it touches an individual is the US-person self-certification banks request, which is tracked with your documents.

scopeNotes.title: Document-upload extraction is simulated
scopeNotes.body: Every "upload to auto-fill" feature in Layer 1 (Form 26AS, Lower-TDS certificate, bank statements, property documents) is a demo simulation with representative values — not live OCR. Figures sourced from an upload should be treated as manually-entered until real extraction ships.

scopeNotes.title: MLI does not affect the India-US treaty
scopeNotes.body: The US never signed the OECD Multilateral Instrument, so the India-US DTAA text is untouched by it — unlike India's treaties with the UK, Netherlands, or Singapore. Verified; nothing to apply.

scopeNotes.title: Treaty text current as modeled
scopeNotes.body: The India-US DTAA has not been amended since the 2000 protocol. Every treaty rate and tie-breaker rule in this engine reflects the treaty as it stands.
